extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, literary scholars, and educated readers interested in principles for evaluating poetry and the conduct of critical journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on evaluating poetry (style, diction, characteristic excellence) and on the proper conduct and principles of periodical criticism. Covers how critics should form and apply canons, avoid personality, and what constitutes poetic excellence in diction and construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair and philosophical investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should announce and endeavor to establish the principles which he holds for the foundation of poetry in general, with the specification of these in their application to the different classes of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare canons of criticism (principles) and then particularize passages to which they apply; faithfully notice the recurrence of merits or defects and distinguish what is characteristic from what is accidental. A fair inquiry is positive (assessing the work on its own terms) rather than merely comparative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive, not comparative, appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Long have I wished to see a fair and philosophical inquisition ... and a positive, not a comparative, appreciation of their characteristic excellences, deficiencies, and defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism aiming to be just should evaluate a poet's works on their own published evidence and identify characteristic qualities rather than only comparing them to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Announce principles and apply them consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic announces and endeavors to establish the principles which he holds for the foundation of poetry, and then proceeds to particularize the most striking passages to which he deems them applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State your evaluative premises clearly; derive deductions legitimately; apply conclusions to specific passages so readers can follow and test the critic's reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish characteristic from accidental merits/defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Faithfully notice the frequent or infrequent recurrence of similar merits or defects, and as faithfully distinguish what is characteristic from what is accidental, or a mere flagging of the wing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving examples, indicate whether a feature is part of the author's constant manner (characteristic) or a one-off occurrence (accidental).

rubrics_metrics.name: Base judgments on published works only; avoid private intimacies
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as the critic betrays that he knows more of his author than the author's publications could have told him; as soon as from this more intimate knowledge he avails himself ... his censure instantly becomes personal injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on private information about an author to support criticism; use only the published text(s) as the basis for judgment to avoid personal insult and unlicensed personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support every censure by the work under review
rubrics_metrics.description: Every censure, every sarcasm respecting a publication which the critic, with the criticised work before him, can make good, is the critic's right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critic may choose tone (soft or bitter) but must be able to substantiate criticisms from the work itself; the writer may reply but not complain of well-supported criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal allusions and revisiting juvenile works as attack
rubrics_metrics.description: I have no quarrel with keenness or asperity ... as long as no personal allusions are admitted, and no re-commitment (for new trial) of juvenile performances, that were published, perhaps forgotten, many years before the commencement of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reintroduce an author's old youthful works to score personal points; criticisms should not be veiled personal assaults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review only works susceptible to argumentative criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Edinburgh Review ... originated the scheme of reviewing those books only, which are susceptible and deserving of argumentative criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus journal space and argumentative effort on books that merit substantive critical engagement; let trivial or mediocre works sink without inflammatory attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use criticism to flatter malignant passions or increase sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjecting to criticism works neither indecent nor immoral, yet of such trumpery importance ... must excite the suspicion either that dislike or vindictive feelings were at work; or that there was a cold prudential pre-determination to increase the sale of the review by flattering the malignant passions of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid selecting targets or tones designed primarily to provoke outrage or boost circulation rather than to advance honest criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic must know the effect he wants and weigh his words accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must know, what effect it is his object to produce; and with a view to this effect must he weigh his words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about rhetorical force: choose language appropriate to the critical aim, balancing severity and fairness to achieve the intended persuasive or corrective effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude unlicensed personality and gossip from criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: He ceases to be a critic, and takes on him the most contemptible character ... that of a gossip, backbiter, and pasquinant: but ... he steals the unquiet, the deforming passions of the world into the museum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid turning criticism into personal invective or gossip; such attacks degrade both critic and literary discourse and violate the sanctity of literary spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground collective critical codes on universal morals and philosophic reason
rubrics_metrics.description: By grounding this code on the two-fold basis of universal morals and philosophic reason, independent of all foreseen application to particular works and authors, they obtain the right to speak each as the representative of their body corporate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If forming an institutional code for criticism (a reviewing body), base it on broadly shared moral and rational principles to legitimate collective pronouncements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid national party bias and personal predilection
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting aside the too manifest and too frequent interference of national party, and even personal predilection or aversion ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for impartiality; do not let national, political, or private biases determine critical judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform adherence to genuine, logical English as a commendable quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The praise of uniform adherence to genuine, logical English is undoubtedly his; nay, having the main emphasis on the word uniform, I will dare add that, of all contemporary poets, 'tis his alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency in clear, logical English is a strong positive quality in a poet's style; it is singled out as a commendable excellence in Wordsworth.

rubrics_metrics.name: An individualized diction can be an essential poetic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory which would establish this lingua 'communis' ... as the only commendable style, should have proceeded from a poet whose diction ... appears to me of all others the most individualized and characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about prescribing one 'common' diction as best; an author's highly individualized diction may be the source of his distinctive beauties and should not be erased by rigid adherence to a prescriptive theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polysyllabic and specialized words may be necessary for precision
rubrics_metrics.description: In The Excursion the number of polysyllabic (or what the common people call, dictionary) words is more than usually great. And so must it needs be, in proportion to the number and variety of an author's conceptions, and his solicitude to express them with precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of learned or polysyllabic vocabulary can be defensible and necessary where complex concepts demand precision; it should not automatically be condemned as 'unpoetic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction need not imitate ordinary spoken language
rubrics_metrics.description: Are those words in those places commonly employed in real life to express the same thought or outward thing? ... No! nor are the modes of connexions; and still less the breaks and transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that poetic constructions, unusual grammar, and figurative turns that differ from everyday speech can be legitimate poetic devices contributing to beauty and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of asyndeton and appositional constructions as poetical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a peculiarity in the frequent use of the asyndeton (that is, the omission of the connective particle before the last of several words ...) and not less in the construction of words by apposition ('to him, a youth').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize such syntactic peculiarities as deliberate stylistic choices that can enhance poetic rhythm and emphasis rather than errors to be corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lines that stand alone as independent beauties
rubrics_metrics.description: I affirm, that from no contemporary writer could so many lines be quoted, without reference to the poem in which they are found, for their own independent weight or beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One measure of poetic excellence can be the frequency with which lines from a poet can be quoted independently and still convey weight and beauty; note such passages when assessing value.
